title: Carstensen et al. (1999): True or False
instructions: Read each statement and choose True or False. Check the explanation against the linked source passage, paying attention to time perspective, study design, and the limits of each finding.

items.prompt: In SST, knowledge-related goals take priority when the future is perceived as open-ended, whereas emotional goals take priority when time is perceived as limited.
items.explanation: The abstract identifies perceived time as fundamental to the selection of social goals. An open-ended future favors knowledge acquisition, while limited time gives emotion-related goals primacy.

items.prompt: SST distinguishes knowledge-related and emotional goals in order to classify behavior as either emotional or nonemotional.
items.explanation: Both classes of goals are essential and overlap. The distinction concerns the primary motive, such as gaining knowledge or satisfying emotional needs; information seeking can involve emotion, and emotional goals can involve information seeking.

items.prompt: The research discussed in the article described older adults as more present-oriented, while the association between age and a focus on the past was not reliable.
items.explanation: The authors emphasize older adults' focus on the here and now, rather than a distant future. They explicitly note that age is not reliably associated with past orientation.

items.prompt: In the incidental-memory study, age differences appeared in the proportion of recalled material that concerned emotional aspects of the situation.
items.explanation: Because overall memory performance differs with age, the authors did not predict that older adults would recall more emotional information in absolute terms. They predicted, and found, that emotional material made up a larger proportion of recall with increasing age.

items.prompt: In the HIV subgroup study, the symptomatic group's greater emphasis on emotional dimensions was explained by its higher average age.
items.explanation: The HIV-negative, HIV-positive asymptomatic, and HIV-positive symptomatic/AIDS subgroups were all male and each had an average age of 37. The design held age comparable while examining differences related to life expectancy.

items.prompt: In the laboratory mood-induction studies reviewed, older adults reported much weaker subjective emotional intensity than younger adults.
items.explanation: Younger and older adults reported comparably intense subjective experiences. This finding is distinct from reports of better control over negative emotions and lower physiological activity among older adults.

items.prompt: The experience-sampling study paged participants aged 18 to 95 at 35 random times over one week and asked them to report on 19 emotional states.
items.explanation: Participants carried electronic pagers and were signaled at random times during the day and evening. At each of the 35 signals, they recorded which of 19 emotional states they were experiencing and how intensely they felt them.

items.prompt: In the experience-sampling findings, both the frequency and intensity of negative emotions decreased with age.
items.explanation: Negative emotions generally declined in frequency, but not in intensity when experienced. Frequency rose somewhat again in very old age without exceeding young-adult levels. Shorter duration of negative emotions, estimated from conditional probabilities, was a separate finding.

items.prompt: In the Child Guidance Study, interaction with spouses, parents, and siblings was maintained or increased while interaction with acquaintances declined.
items.explanation: Participants were interviewed at ages 18, 30, 40, and 50. Interaction rates with acquaintances and satisfaction with those contacts declined, while interaction rates with spouses, parents, and siblings remained stable or increased.

items.prompt: The Berlin Aging Study analysis described in the article established individual network shrinkage by following the same participants over many years.
items.explanation: The reported analysis was a cross-sectional comparison of adults aged 69 to 104. It found fewer peripheral partners among the oldest adults but similar numbers of emotionally close partners; the design does not establish within-person developmental change.

items.prompt: When participants imagined an approaching geographical move, younger adults' social-partner preferences became indistinguishable from older adults' preferences.
items.explanation: Younger adults showed no preference for familiar partners in the baseline condition. When the imagined move constrained time, they favored familiar partners, as older adults did in both conditions.

items.prompt: Imagining a medical breakthrough that would likely add 20 years to life eliminated older adults' preference for familiar partners, leaving them no more likely than younger adults to prefer those partners.
items.explanation: Younger adults' preferences were stable across conditions. Older adults favored familiar partners at baseline, but that bias disappeared when they imagined an expanded future.

items.prompt: One year after Hong Kong's handover, younger and older adults continued to show the same shared preference for familiar partners observed shortly before the handover.
items.explanation: Four months before the handover, both younger and older adults preferred familiar partners. One year afterward, the association between age and partner preference again resembled the pattern observed one year before the handover.

items.prompt: The authors describe SST as complementing SOC by specifying which goals are selected in social and emotional domains.
items.explanation: SOC describes the general processes of selection, optimization, and compensation without prescribing specific developmental goals. SST supplies predictions about prioritizing emotional goals and selecting meaningful social partners when time is limited.

items.prompt: The clinical discussion presents an efficacy trial demonstrating that a present-focused approach treats depression near the end of life.
items.explanation: The authors explicitly describe this therapeutic possibility as conjecture. They suggest that a present focus may help some distressed people approaching the end of life, but do not present a treatment trial establishing its efficacy.
